To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) glucose concentrations above 5.6 mm in the absence of hormonal stimulation result in glycogen deposition in cultured rat liver parenchytal cells, 2) the addition of insulin to the culture medium results in a 15 to 25% increase in cellular glycogen content at medium glucose concentrations greater than or equal to 10.6 mm, and 3) the addition of glucocorticoids to the culture medium stimulates glycogen deposition in a dose‐dependent manner at
glucose concentrations greater than physiological (10.6 mM), insulin, and glucocorticoids stimulate glycogen deposition by rat liver parenchymeal cells in vitro.

the addition of glucocorticoids to the culture medium of rat liver paren­ chymal cells results in a 50 to 105% increase in glycogen deposition in cells grown at glucose concentrations greater that 10.6mM.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hormonal and nutritional regulation of glycogen deposition in rat liver parenchormal cells maintained in a serum‐free culture system.
the effect of the hormones insulin and glucocorticoids on the metabolism of glucose and glycogen in primary cultures of adult rat liver parenchyamal cells.
the regulation of glycogen deposition in rat liver parenchymeal cells maintained in vitro in chemically defined media.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glucocorticoids stimulate glycogen deposition, but the effect is dependent on the presence of glucose and insulin.

the glucocorticoid hormones and insulin stimulate glycogen deposition only when the medium glucose concentration is above 10.0 mM, but that glucose concentrations above physiological levels stimulate glycogen deposition even in the absence of these hormones.
the addition of glucocorticoids and insulin together in a chemically well‐defined medium stimulates glycogen deposition in a synergistic manner at glucose concentrations above 5.6mM.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glucose, insulin, and glucocorticoids all stimulate glycogen deposition.
glucocorticoids and insulin stimulate glycogen deposition only when glucose is present in excess of 10.6mM.
the glucocorticoid‐stimulated increase in glycogen deposition in rat liver parenchymeal cells is dependent upon the availability of glucose in the medium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
glucocorticoids are the most important hormones in stimulating glycogen deposition in liver parenchyma cells.
glucocorticoid treatment of adult liver parenchyma cells in primary culture results in increased cellular glycogen deposition in a dose‐dependent fashion.
glucocorticoids can stimulate glycogen deposition by two mechanisms, namely by increasing glucose utilization and by increasing the rate of glycogen synthesis.
